sessions.title: AI Without the Jargon: You Have Already Used It Today
sessions.what: Spot-the-AI stand/sit game (eight items, including a calculator trap), rules-versus-examples idea using the spam filter, live demo with requests from the floor (one useful, one silly, one false-premise trap), pairs on their own phones with task cards, myth-buster line. The explanation of what the tool is doing comes only after the board is read.
sessions.walkaway: One useful chat on your own phone; a one-sentence definition; five things to try tonight
sessions.tools: Any free chatbot on a phone
sessions.target: Exit poll: at least 80% agree with each of: "I can explain AI in one sentence", "I will try it this week", "I would come back".

sessions.title: The Prompt Recipe
sessions.what: Worst Prompt Wins warm-up, then rewrite one prompt a letter at a time using the club recipe (Context, Role, Task, Format, then Tweak); same task on three chatbots side by side (a blind taste test with answers shown as A, B, C, then tools revealed); a meme-led opener on common ways people use AI wrong; prompt makeover; fact-check pause.
sessions.walkaway: A personal prompt card with five reusable prompts and a chart of which tool for which job

sessions.title: How Machines Learn
sessions.what: Paper cards first (unbalanced, then varied examples), then Teachable Machine with two classes from members' own interests; break-it challenge (background, angle); next-word game linking to chatbots.
sessions.walkaway: A model you trained and broke; a ten-year-old-test definition of training data

sessions.title: Human or AI? Game Night
sessions.what: Teams of four judge club-written versus AI texts, image pairs, a beat-the-bot round and Two Truths and a Hallucination. A 50% chance line goes on the board before round one and the room's real score is set beside it. The tells list is built from what actually fooled people.
sessions.walkaway: A list of tells; three new people met
sessions.buildsOn: Revisits Sessions 1 to 3 (play sessions revisit earlier material; 3 + 1 rhythm)

sessions.title: Confidently Wrong: Catching the Mistakes
sessions.what: Hallucination face-off with planted errors; case files labelled supported, contradicted or not enough evidence; a plot-twist claim with a subtle flaw; the three-step check (specific claim? second source? does it change if asked again?).
sessions.walkaway: A wallet card with the three-step check; Hall of Fails entries
sessions.tools: Chatbot, search engine, printed case files

sessions.title: Research Partner and Study Lab
sessions.what: Four-step workflow Scope, Search, Ground, Synthesise; NotebookLM on members' own course notes; Perplexity with citations; click every citation; rule "no source, no sentence"; academic-integrity slide quoting the college policy.
sessions.walkaway: A study assistant for one real course and a one-page sourced brief

sessions.title: Messy Data to a Decision
sessions.what: A deliberately messy file (for example a quick-commerce mystery set or NIRF/placement data) cleaned with AI help, asked questions in plain English, turned into a pivot and one chart with a one-line takeaway.
sessions.walkaway: A clean sheet, a chart and one defensible recommendation
sessions.tools: Sheets or Excel with Gemini, ChatGPT data analysis, Quadratic

sessions.title: Senior versus Machine and Hot Takes Night
sessions.what: Four final-year students and a chatbot answer the same questions; then a spectrum debate on "Would you let AI…?" with an AI devil's-advocate round. Neutral facilitator, light non-political statements.
sessions.walkaway: A clear sense of what machines cannot answer; everyone speaks once
sessions.tools: Floor tape, sticky notes, one device
sessions.buildsOn: Revisits Sessions 5 to 7 (play sessions revisit earlier material; 3 + 1 rhythm)

sessions.title: The 10-Minute Analyst: Read Any Annual Report
sessions.what: Pairs choose a listed company, find its annual report, run two routes side by side (NotebookLM on the document versus Perplexity without it), answer six questions, verify one number against the report, ask the tool what its own summary misses.
sessions.walkaway: A one-page brief and one number verified at source

sessions.title: Problem First: Campus Case Night
sessions.what: Teams act as consultants on a short case (for example delivery-time prediction, product recommendation, recruitment, demand forecasting): problem, how AI helps, data needed, risks, success measure. An industry guest joins by video as judge. Then an Annoyance Auction of campus pain points; winning problems become Problem Cards.
sessions.walkaway: A Problem Card each team carries to the capstone

sessions.title: Idea Sprint and AI Sharks
sessions.what: Sketch a solution to your Problem Card yourself, then make AI attack it as a sceptical investor, a user and a competitor. Pitch for 90 seconds to three AI "sharks" with different personas; the human audience votes. Five questions to ask a real person before building.
sessions.walkaway: A one-page concept note v2 and a booked real-person interview

sessions.title: Zero Rupee Consultant: Crack a Case in 90 Minutes
sessions.what: Invented campus-cafe case labelled as invented; paper-only block with phones shut; devices open at minute 25; a planted authoritative-sounding false market claim; two-minute pitches to a senior or faculty judge; scorecards returned. Opened to two outside teams online as a rehearsal for Neural Fest.
sessions.walkaway: Three recommendations with numbers; the reveal of who caught the planted claim
sessions.target: Share of teams that catch the planted false claim (measure named in V1-09; no number given in the document).
sessions.buildsOn: Revisits Sessions 9 to 11 (play sessions revisit earlier material; 3 + 1 rhythm)

sessions.title: Does the Algorithm Like You? Bias Lab
sessions.what: Train and deliberately break a small model; ask a chatbot to describe "a doctor", "a leader", "a typical student"; ask the same open question ten times and read the patterns; garbage in, garbage out.
sessions.walkaway: The club's five AI Do's and Don'ts

sessions.title: Your Data, Your Rights, and AI on Your Own Laptop
sessions.what: Phone privacy clean-up; what should never leave your machine; the questions an app should be able to answer under India's data protection law (dates re-checked the week before); a small local model answering with wifi off (model file passed round on a pen drive); a five-point tool scorecard.
sessions.walkaway: A clean-up checklist, a scorecard and a local model that works offline
sessions.tools: A local-model app, pen drive, phone settings

sessions.title: Deepfakes, Scams and Authenticity
sessions.what: Spot-the-fake with deepfakes and misleading charts; UPI-fraud and voice-clone scenarios; a labelling debate. Output is a family safety card people forward the same night.
sessions.walkaway: A family safety card

sessions.title: AI on Trial: Courtroom and Debate Night
sessions.what: Mock trial with The Dialectical Society (prosecution, defence, witnesses, jury; cases on employment, creativity and ownership, recruitment, accountability) or a vote-with-your-feet debate with random sides and a mid-round switch. Argue first without AI, then use AI as a sparring partner.
sessions.walkaway: Both sides of an ethics question, argued and voted
sessions.buildsOn: Revisits Sessions 13 to 15 (play sessions revisit earlier material; 3 + 1 rhythm)

sessions.title: Kill One Boring Task: No-Code Automation Lab
sessions.what: Live "magic trick" demo, then trigger, condition, action; guided build of form to sheet to automation tool to an AI-written confirmation; Automation Menu (weekly summary, deadline tracker, email sorter, attendance logger); a break-it swap; the "worth it" rule (time saved times frequency against time to build).
sessions.walkaway: One working automation and a worth-it rule
sessions.tools: Google Forms and Sheets; Zapier, Make or Apps Script
sessions.target: 80% of pairs with a working flow at minute 70 and 95% at the end; a poll two weeks later asks whether people still use it.

sessions.title: Where the Money Goes
sessions.what: Budget against a real month (invented figures on screen, private entry), EMI with the PMT function, flat versus reducing balance, credit-score basics, a small calculator built and tested against the hand calculation. Closes with an honest limit: a tutor, not an adviser. A finance-club member checks the calculator first.
sessions.walkaway: A budget and a tested calculator

sessions.title: Vibe Coding 101: Build a Tool by Describing It
sessions.what: Describe a small campus tool (mess-menu rating, fest countdown); a free AI app builder writes it; test, ask for changes in words, share a working link. Game design in three words: goal, points, surprise.
sessions.walkaway: A working single-page tool that opens on a phone
sessions.tools: A free AI app builder or coding assistant

sessions.title: Creative Lab
sessions.what: Pick from the session bank: AI Relay (build, pass, transform in 15-minute rounds), Chaos Room (bizarre prompts, guess the prompt, fictional movie poster), Meme Lab, Sound Studio, 60-second film. Consent ground rules read aloud.
sessions.walkaway: A gallery of member-made work
sessions.tools: Free image, text and audio tools
sessions.buildsOn: Revisits Sessions 17 to 19 (play sessions revisit earlier material; 3 + 1 rhythm)

sessions.title: Your Marketing Team of One
sessions.what: An ad auction with fake money (media slots, sponsorships, influencers, shock cards), then AI used to build a campaign for one real campus event: a week of posts, a deck, a poster, a short film and a voice script. Nothing is posted before the Media Cell has seen it.
sessions.walkaway: One finished campaign for a real event

sessions.title: Assistants, Agents and the Back Office
sessions.what: Teach It Once (a custom assistant fed your own notes), a supervised agent doing a multi-step task with a log of what you approved, and a payroll or accounts workflow where the machine does three steps and a named person signs the fourth. RAG explained through your own documents.
sessions.walkaway: A saved assistant, an agent log and a signed-off workflow
sessions.tools: Projects, custom GPTs or Gems, Apps Script

sessions.title: Capstone Build Day
sessions.what: See V1-10.
sessions.walkaway: A working prototype and a three-slide pitch
sessions.target: Most teams submit a working demo; most members report building something for the first time (no number given in the document).
sessions.buildsOn: Session 10 (Problem Cards) and Session 11 (concept note v2)

sessions.title: Neural Fest and Demo Day
sessions.what: See V1-11.
sessions.walkaway: A finished project, a certificate by level and a reason to return
sessions.buildsOn: Session 23 (Build Day prototypes); Session 12 is the online rehearsal

1.title: AI Without the Jargon
1.fullTitle: AI Without the Jargon: You Have Already Used It Today
1.duration: 60 minutes, up to 80 in the hall, teams of four
1.audience: Up to 80 in the hall, in teams of four. Entry sessions assume no account, laptop or prior knowledge (V1-01).

timed.what: Eight items (spam filter, calculator, maps ETA, face unlock, autocorrect, thermostat, streaming suggestions, chatbot); stand for AI, sit for not. The calculator catches people out.

Rules versus examples: a spam filter used to be a list of banned words, now it has learned from millions of emails; like showing a child 100 dogs, not writing a rulebook. One sentence at about minute 45 that a spam filter and a chatbot are different kinds of tool.
One useful request (a two-day trip plan on a student budget), one silly (GST explained as a hostel warden would), one trap (a false premise).
Task cards: plan a free Sunday; explain a topic from your branch to a ten-year-old; ask something it cannot know. Green notes for hits, orange for misses.

Stand on a line for "it is just a search engine", "it knows everything", "it is conscious", "it will take all jobs", "only coders can use it". Honest nuance, not slogans. Then say what it is doing: guessing what comes next from patterns.
Sticky note: one thing I will try this week; five things to try tonight; announce Session 2 and ask people to bring a photograph of something unreadable.

1.activities: Spot-the-AI stand/sit game (eight items, including a calculator trap), rules-versus-examples idea using the spam filter, live demo with requests from the floor (one useful, one silly, one false-premise trap), pairs on their own phones with task cards, myth-buster line. The explanation of what the tool is doing comes only after the board is read.
1.tools: Any free chatbot on a phone
1.learn: One useful chat on your own phone; a one-sentence definition; five things to try tonight
1.resources: Printed task cards, sticky notes (green for hits, orange for misses), a projector, phones. A recording made the day before as backup. Classroom or hall for 30 to 80, seated in fours (Section 2.8).
1.outcomes: It worked if most teams can describe one wrong answer they got and most of the room has had a first useful conversation on their own phone. Exit poll targets: 80% agreement on each of three statements.
1.engage: Door game with stand and sit; the calculator catches people out; live demo with requests from the floor; myth-buster line where people stand on a line; one sticky-note commitment to leave with.
1.prep: Programme-wide (V1-01): write the one-sentence promise, run the beginner test-run, vet tools, prepare the paper fallback, one week before.
1.risks: If it goes wrong: network down, play a recording made the day before and run the guessing game on paper; the tool refuses something, that becomes the lesson.
1.roles: Programme-wide (V1-01): a lead host, co-host, two floaters and a note-taker per session.

4.title: Human or AI? Game Night
4.audience: Teams of four. Play (chill) session, no scoring pressure on beginners; first-timers are a stated focus of play sessions (V1-04).

timed.what: Teams choose names; scoring on screen; the 50% chance line goes up before round one.

Six to ten pairs of texts (a canteen poem, an apology to a professor, a LinkedIn post, a leave application, a couplet). Club members wrote one of each pair, collected anonymously two weeks earlier; the other is machine-made. Reveal with 30 seconds on the tells.

timed.segment: Round 2: Fool the room / describe-off / images
timed.what: Teams write two lines and quietly have a machine write two more; fooling a team scores double. Or one player gets a secret item and must make the AI describe it without forbidden words. Image pairs with openly licensed real photos.

Show the supposed giveaways, then the room's real score against the 50% line. Make the AI do something ridiculous (wedding vows from a samosa to chai); applause meter plus a bonus for the best one-line prompt.
What did we notice? What would you never let it write for you? Stickers or coupons; invite everyone to the next session.

4.activities: Teams of four judge club-written versus AI texts, image pairs, a beat-the-bot round and Two Truths and a Hallucination. A 50% chance line goes on the board before round one and the room's real score is set beside it. The tells list is built from what actually fooled people.
4.learn: A list of tells; three new people met
4.resources: Cards, scoreboard, slides, small prizes (stickers or coupons). Ten human-written texts and ten machine-made ones on the same subjects, shuffled. Openly licensed real photos for image pairs. Quizzar runs scoring and the microphone if it agrees (V2-07).
4.engage: Teams choose names; the 50% chance line goes on the board before round one and the room's real score is set beside it; applause meter and a bonus for the best one-line prompt; awards; an invitation to the next session.
4.prep: A week ahead: write ten human texts, generate ten machine ones on the same subjects, shuffle. Club members write one of each pair, collected anonymously two weeks earlier.
4.risks: Safeguards: every origin revealed after each vote; no real person's photograph, voice or name; detectors are never used to accuse anyone. Keep a paper version in case devices fail (V1-04).
4.roles: Play Lead and a host pool (V1-04); neutral facilitator for any debate segment.

12.title: Zero Rupee Consultant
12.fullTitle: Zero Rupee Consultant: Crack a Case in 90 Minutes
12.duration: 90 minutes, teams of four or five
12.audience: Teams of four or five, BMS and MBA mixed, first years with seniors (V1-09). Opened to two outside teams online as a rehearsal for Neural Fest.

timed.what: An invented campus-cafe case labelled as invented; rule on the board: nothing switched on during the paper block.
Read the numbers, find where the money goes, write a one-sentence hypothesis.
Size the opportunity and test the hypothesis against the numbers.
Release an authoritative-sounding market claim that contradicts the sales sheet. Nobody is told it is wrong.
Two minutes of pitch.
Two minutes each, one question from the judge.
Which teams caught the planted claim. Scorecards go back to every team.

12.activities: Invented campus-cafe case labelled as invented; paper-only block with phones shut; devices open at minute 25; a planted authoritative-sounding false market claim; two-minute pitches to a senior or faculty judge; scorecards returned. Opened to two outside teams online as a rehearsal for Neural Fest.
12.learn: Three recommendations with numbers; the reveal of who caught the planted claim
12.resources: Case pack, rubric, timer, hall (Section 2.8). A senior or faculty judge; judges are recruited by Outreach (V1-09, V2-04, V2-05).
12.outcomes: Measure named in V1-09: the share of teams catching the planted claim. The document gives no number. The reveal is the lesson: the teams that checked the claim against their own numbers win.
12.engage: Paper-only block with phones shut; devices open at minute 25; a planted authoritative-sounding false claim that nobody is told is wrong; scorecards go back to every team; the reveal.
12.prep: V1-09: write each case in plain English with every term footnoted and invented figures marked invented; no real campus vendor is analysed; brief judges in advance; publish the rubric.
12.risks: Provide a paper version if the network fails. If only twelve turn up: a case competition with two teams and one judge (Section 4.8).
12.roles: Case Lead (V1-09); a senior or faculty judge; hosts from the pool.

17.title: Kill One Boring Task
17.fullTitle: Kill One Boring Task: No-Code Automation Lab
17.duration: About 120 minutes, pairs with floating helpers
17.audience: Pairs, Builder level, with floating helpers at each table.

timed.what: Submit a form on stage; a phone buzzes in ten seconds and a sheet updates; the audience guesses how.

Trigger, condition, action, with student examples (assignment email to calendar event; form submission to message; every Sunday a summary of notes). The AI step is the smart bit in the middle that reads, summarises or classifies.

Four checkpoints with helpers at each table and green or red cups for help: make a form; link it to a sheet; connect a free automation tool to send a confirmation; add the AI step to write a personalised confirmation.
Pick from the Automation Menu: notes to weekly summary, deadline tracker, email sorter, attendance logger, mess-menu reminder.
Swap laptops; try an empty form, a very long answer, a wrong email; fix what breaks.
The worth-it rule; privacy and password reminder; plan the next build.

17.activities: Live "magic trick" demo, then trigger, condition, action; guided build of form to sheet to automation tool to an AI-written confirmation; Automation Menu (weekly summary, deadline tracker, email sorter, attendance logger); a break-it swap; the "worth it" rule (time saved times frequency against time to build).
17.tools: Google Forms and Sheets; Zapier, Make or Apps Script
17.learn: One working automation and a worth-it rule
17.resources: Laptops (keyboard session: teams of three or four around one machine, or a lab, if laptops are short), a free automation tool, a written step-by-step guide, a three-minute backup video, a sign-up checklist sent three days earlier.
17.outcomes: 80% of pairs with a working flow at minute 70 and 95% at the end; a poll two weeks later asks whether people still use it.
17.engage: A live magic-trick hook where a phone buzzes in ten seconds; green or red cups to call for help; an Automation Menu to choose from; a break-it swap of laptops.
17.prep: Build and test the flow twice; list free-tier limits; write a step-by-step guide and record a three-minute backup video; send a sign-up checklist three days earlier.
17.risks: Network down: paper versions, a pre-recorded demo, hotspots (Section 4.8). Tools change or lock: vet tools a week before and 24 hours before, keep a backup tool and screenshots.
17.roles: Floating helpers at each table (checkpoint helpers at four checkpoints). Role holders are not named in the document for this session.

23.title: Capstone Build Day
23.duration: A full day. Check-in at 10:00, submission at 16:00.
23.audience: Up to about fifteen teams of three or four, mixing second years and juniors.
23.objective: Let everyone who joined at zero build something and show it to a room in a single day.

timed.what: No-code or low-code, honest about limits.
With a mentor.
Mentors rotating every 20 minutes.
A 60-second halfway show.
Submission at 16:00.
Three-minute demos with two minutes for questions, scored on usefulness and clarity.
Judging while the audience votes.
Awards, group photo and a recap of the year. Each team names one way its tool could be misused before the awards.

23.activities: Tracks: study, campus life, business and operations, creative work, and data on a public dataset. Schedule: 10:00 check-in and rules (no-code or low-code, honest about limits); tool refresher and problem check with a mentor; build sprint 1 with mentors rotating every 20 minutes; lunch and a 60-second halfway show; build sprint 2 with submission at 16:00; three-minute demos with two for questions, scored on usefulness and clarity; judging while the audience votes; awards, group photo and a recap of the year. Each team names one way its tool could be misused before the awards. Starter kits for stalled teams. Optional launch lane for teams that want a live link: put the code in a repository and publish through a free host, supported by Maker Track coaches.
23.learn: A working prototype and a three-slide pitch
23.resources: Large hall with long tables, power strips, wifi plus hotspot backup, mentor list, submission form, judging sheet, prizes, starter kits.
23.outcomes: Most teams submit a working demo; most members report building something for the first time. Measured by: Share of teams submitting a demo; share of members reporting a first build; judge scores; audience vote participation.
23.engage: Mentors rotate every 20 minutes; a halfway show; an audience vote alongside the judges; starter kits for stalled teams; awards and a group photo.
23.prep: Four weeks out: confirm hall, power strips, backup hotspots, mentors, judges and prizes (with Outreach, V2-09). | Two weeks out: teams form from Problem Cards; scope to a one-day version. | On the day: follow the schedule; judging sheet rewards clarity and honesty about limits as much as polish. | Within five days: recap, thank-yous to mentors and sponsors, and a published list of projects.
23.risks: Starter kits for stalled teams; wifi plus a hotspot backup; the judging sheet rewards clarity and honesty about limits as much as polish.
23.roles: Projects Lead (owner); Outreach Lead for judges, sponsors and prizes; mentors from seniors and alumni.

cadence: Cadence. Two flagship sessions a month. Between sessions, a thin weekly layer keeps momentum: a one-page takeaway and a three-question recall quiz in the club group, a weekly "Did you know?" post and one optional niche mission. Teams that want a faster pace may add weekly sessions from Term 2 if Session 4 turnout holds at about 60% of Session 1.

Exam rule. No sessions in roughly ten days around mid-sems and end-sems; a "pre-exam detox" play session just before study week; in exam months swap heavy sessions for chill or 45-minute ones instead of cancelling.
Duration. Core sessions 75 to 90 minutes; play sessions 45 to 75 minutes; Session 17 about two hours; Session 23 a full day.

Fallback. If the calendar will not hold 24, the protected twelve are Sessions 1, 3, 4, 6, 7, 9, 12, 15, 18, 20, 21 and 23. The mix survives (opener, asking properly, checking, spreadsheet, annual report, case competition, scam safety, money, marketing, build day) even though the every-fourth rhythm does not. The decision rule is: if fewer than one in three of Session 1 attendees are still coming by Session 12, announce the switch to the club group instead of letting the year shrink silently.

indicators.target: Session 12 at least 70% of Session 1; Session 4 at about 60% of Session 1 triggers the option of weekly sessions
If under one third of Session 1 attendees remain by Session 12
80% of exit tickets state the key idea (for example "patterns from data, not looking up facts")
90% agree "I learned a use I did not know"; average rating 4 or above
Average 1-to-5 confidence at Session 23 above Session 1
Share of attendees who spoke at least once; spotlights claimed rising each term
Entries from most members, not just a few
Most members or squads present a finished project; real-person feedback quotes collected
80% working flow by minute 70, 95% at the end; still in use after two weeks

outcomes: Members can explain AI in plain words, write a clear prompt, check a claim and protect their data.
A cohort with shipped projects, portfolio pages and, for the Maker Track, live links.
A living Field Guide, a monthly Radar and a case library that outlast the first cohort.
A culture where beginners teach, quiet members contribute and failure is shared openly (Hall of Fails).
A calendar of events that Outreach can sell to partners with confidence.

items.t: Take a beginner from first prompt to a shipped project in four terms, with every session self-contained and every term harder than the last.

fields.label: Why the club should do it

items.t: The curation plan follows a progressive, hands-on, beginner-first arc (use, then understand, then apply, then build). A single spine avoids duplicating sessions and gives Outreach a calendar to plan speakers and judges against.
All IIM Sirmaur students, BMS first (up to MBA students for the harder questions). Entry sessions assume no account, laptop or prior knowledge.
The 24 sessions in Section 2.4; six play sessions; between-session layer; session bank for rotation (V1-04).
Confirm dates two terms ahead against the academic calendar.
Assign a lead host, co-host, two floaters and a note-taker per session.
One week before: write the one-sentence promise, run the beginner test-run, vet tools, prepare the paper fallback.
On the day: follow the blueprint (V1-02).
Next morning: file the one-page session record (V1-14) and the recap (V2-12).
Projector, room, printed cards, QR codes, free tool accounts, snacks for play sessions; no paid tools.
Curation Lead (owner); Session Host Pool; Programme Coordinator for dates and rooms; Faculty Advisor for approval.
Twice a month for twelve months from launch; terms of about three months.
A cohort that can explain AI, check its output, apply it to coursework and cases, and has shipped something.
Attendance by session; exit-slip comprehension (target 80% on the key idea); return rate between sessions; number of members with a finished artefact by Session 24.
Give every host one proven shape for a session so that quality does not depend on who is running it.

fields.label: Why the club should do it

items.t: The strongest sessions share a recognisable rhythm. A common blueprint lets two students with a projector run most sessions and makes new hosts productive quickly.
Session hosts, co-hosts and floaters; indirectly, every attendee.

Core blueprint (90 min): 5 min context capsule and recap quiz; 10 min The Problem (a story or poll, "raise your hand if this happened to you"); 15 min The Idea (one concept, plain language, maximum eight slides); 30 to 35 min Try It (pairs, everyone makes something); 5 min play break; 5 min Reality Check (hallucination, bias, privacy, over-trust); and a closing "Should we?" question on whether what was learned or built ought to be used and where it could harm; 15 min share-back and exit slip. Play blueprint (60 to 75 min): teams and rules, three or four rounds, a reveal that carries the hidden lesson, awards, a one-minute takeaway from each team.

Every session also carries: a one-sentence promise; a "something breaks on purpose, then a reveal" moment; a zero-background analogy; a take-home card; roles named for host, presenter, support and floaters; and "if it goes wrong" and "it worked if" lines.
Publish the blueprint as a one-page template in the Field Guide.
Host drafts a run-sheet in the template, with timings.
A complete beginner test-runs the draft and flags jargon.
Host rehearses once with the team.
Facilitator language rule: say "the model predicts / was trained on / generated", not "the AI thinks / wants / understands".
Run-sheet template; prompt recipe poster; exit-slip form with QR code; printed analogy cards.
Curation Lead owns the template; Session Host Pool uses it; Beginner Tester (rotating volunteer).
Template set up before Session 1; refreshed at the mid-year review.
Consistent, welcoming sessions; shorter prep; fewer overruns; easier handover.
Share of sessions with a complete run-sheet filed; exit-slip scores; beginner test-run completed for every draft.

initiatives.title: Level Pathways and the Between-Session Layer

items.t: Let a beginner and someone already comfortable with AI both find value, and keep learning alive in the gaps between sessions.

fields.label: Why the club should do it

items.t: Someone who already uses AI should still find something useful; a two-week gap can undo learning; and there should be no mandatory follow-up work. The solution is optional, light and levelled.
All members; Explorer, Builder and Maker levels; A four-step level key maps to these.

Level tags on every session; a one-page takeaway and three-question recall quiz after each session; a weekly "Did you know?" post; one optional niche or task mission in the group chat; two small activities between some sessions; a catch-up page so absentees can rejoin.
Tag each session Explorer, Builder or Maker.
After each session, post the takeaway card and quiz within 24 hours.
Each Monday, post one Did-you-know (a capability or tool tip).
Open each session with a two-minute recap quiz so newcomers catch up.
Missed a session? Use the catch-up page; async Duo Swap is allowed.
Group chat, quiz tool or form, Field Guide pages.
Content and Field Guide Editor; Curation Lead for levels.
Weekly posts; takeaway after every session.
Continuity across gaps; level clarity; no mandatory homework.
Quiz completion rate; share of attendees who report trying one thing between sessions; return rate.

initiatives.title: Play Sessions and the Session Bank

items.t: Hold six well-run play sessions a year, each with a real lesson hidden inside, and keep a bank of tried formats so no play session has to be invented from scratch.

fields.label: Why the club should do it

items.t: Every plan includes play, but it is easy to treat it as an afterthought. Play sessions need a tight run-of-show to avoid feeling unplanned. Retention depends on first-timers making friends.
All members; first-timers especially.

Six play sessions (4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24), each closing a block of learning. The session bank keeps formats from the wider idea pool for rotation or for extra sessions: AI Escape Room that revisits Term 1 skills; AI Film Festival; AI Treasure Hunt; AI Quiz Battle and Trivia Night; Movie Night with a Real-or-Hollywood scorecard; Meme Lab; AI Relay; AI Unleashed with random-word and constraint rounds; Chaos Room; Guess the Team Member reel; Sound Studio; Capability Carnival with five stations and a passport; Data Detective guess-before-you-look; Build-a-Bot Battle; AI Mythbusters and Hallucination Museum; Deepfake Detective; Prompt Wars Pictionary; Turing Test Mafia; Bug Bash and AI Quiz Show; Show and Tell with failure stories; Debate Night with AI; Pre-exam detox session; Human Takeover campus challenge, AI After Hours discussion, AI versus Human Challenge and Should AI Make the Decision?; AI Art Arena with Nostalgia Recreated and Campus of the Future; AI campus challenge with slogans and product ads; Human x AI Creative Playground with a non-digital route; Orientation icebreaker where an AI introduces my partner, plus a Human or AI? warm-up and a note of what each member wants to learn and what makes them nervous (held before Session 1).
Choose each play session from the bank at least a month ahead and book it in the calendar.
Prepare material a week ahead where needed (for example collecting human-written samples).
Use ground rules: consent first, kind humour, no real people's photos, voices or names, no voice cloning, existing songs only as inspiration.
Use a neutral facilitator and de-escalation phrases for debates.
Keep a paper version in case devices fail.
Cards, scoreboard, slides, small prizes (stickers or coupons), a hall for competitions, a neutral moderator.
Play Lead (a member of the Curation team); Session Host Pool; campus clubs for co-delivery (see V2-07).
Every fourth session; extra bank formats may be used as short openers (10-minute game).
Retention, friendships, revision through play, and a body of public-facing fun content.
Return rate after a play session; friends brought; share of attendees who spoke at least once; one-question rating.
Turn members from audience into contributors: they choose topics, teach each other, earn visible credit for effort and are recognised by peers.

fields.label: Why the club should do it

items.t: Interest-led peer teaching keeps a mixed-ability club engaged; grouping by niche keeps beginners interested; and evidence suggests that teaching others improves learning. Recognition by effort rather than expertise lets beginners top the board.
All members; quiet members through non-presenting roles.

Spark Board and Spark Card (three things I am curious about and one thing I would love to make); Duo Swap (Spark, Pair, Learn, Teach using the ten-year-old rule, Remix, Log; partners rotate each term; async version if a partner is absent); Volunteer Spotlight five-minute slots claimed a week ahead; quiet-member roles (Field Guide editor, timekeeper, question-asker, tool tester); interest pods of three to five by niche, with a niche pack of five everyday tasks prepared by curators and a core-plus-niche layer in selected sessions; Goal Wall and sealed envelopes opened at the final session, with before-and-after one-sentence definitions of AI; member-led segments in later sessions after rehearsal; whole member-led sessions deferred to year two; points and levels: attend 2, share in Wins and Faceplants 2, Spotlight 10, Duo Swap 10, Field Guide entry 5, help someone 5, game win 5, milestone 15, real-person test 20, bring a friend 5; levels Neuron 0, Synapse 40, Network 100, Deep Learner 180; cap of 40 points per member per session; peer-voted season awards (Curious Cat, Best Explainer, Faceplant Hero, Team Player, Rising Star, People's Choice); a live leaderboard with season totals.
Month 0: open the Spark Board and niche form (four questions).
Session 1: collect Spark Cards and Goal Cards; form first pairs and pods.
Each term: rotate partners; run a Spotlight sign-up a week before each session.
Keep the leaderboard in a shared sheet; points confirmed by a partner or host.
Term finales: peer-voted awards.
Review points weights after the first four sessions (the level thresholds are a starting guess).
Shared sheet with formulas, noticeboard or digital board, printed cards, sticky notes, envelopes, certificates or badges.
Community Lead (owner); Programme Coordinator for the leaderboard; Field Guide Editor for entries.
Continuous; partner rotation each term; awards at each term finale.
A club where beginners teach, quiet members contribute and the same few voices do not dominate.
Spotlights claimed per term (rising); Field Guide entries from most members; share of members completing at least one Duo Swap; leaderboard spread (no run-away leader, thanks to the cap).

initiatives.title: Club Field Guide and Knowledge Repository

items.t: Keep everything the club learns in one living, searchable place that the next cohort inherits.

fields.label: Why the club should do it

items.t: The Field Guide is the memory of the club; a Prompt Cookbook by niche sits alongside it; a page is produced after every session; and a shared template keeps outputs comparable. Together they give the research function something concrete to curate.
Members, hosts and the incoming committee; selected pages public for the wider campus.

Sections: prompts that worked (with prompt, result and why); Prompt Cookbook sorted by niche; tool review cards (what each tool is good and bad at); myths busted and Fact-versus-Fiction page; Hall of Fails with case files; plain-words glossary with ten-year-old-test definitions; session records and recaps; case library of Problem Cards and campus cases; AI Do's and Don'ts; Domain Brief template; weekly Did-you-know archive; "What I decided against" log of rejected ideas and reasons; project portfolio pages; Field Guide v1.0 at mid-year and v2.0 handed to next year.
Choose a simple shared home (shared document or workspace) before Session 1.
Give each session a template page filled in the next morning.
Pairs write one Field Guide card per Duo Swap; the Field Guide Editor confirms and tags it.
Quarterly clean-up: merge duplicates, retire outdated tool pages.
Publish the public subset (myths busted, prompts that worked) with member consent (V2-12).
Shared workspace, templates, an editor role, consent form for public content.
Content and Field Guide Editor (owner); Curation Lead; pairs as authors.
Updated after every session; reviewed quarterly.
A durable knowledge base; faster onboarding; raw material for content and for case work.
Accepted entries per term and share of members contributing; pages reused in later sessions; Field Guide visits.
Keep the programme current and honest: vet tools, check claims, and publish a monthly view of what changed in AI.

fields.label: Why the club should do it

items.t: AI tools and free tiers change constantly, so checking before each session is essential. A research standard stops sessions being built on viral posts.
Session hosts and the whole club; Outreach for briefing partners.

AI Radar: a short monthly round-up of new features, free-tier changes and risks, feeding content. Tool vetting checklist: free? works on phones? needs a credit card? privacy acceptable? has a backup? verified a week before and again 24 hours before. Lightweight research standard: use identifiable sources (tool documentation, reputable educational material, research papers for technical claims, credible reporting for current developments), check dates, separate verified facts, opinions and illustrative fiction, and avoid untraceable statistics. Facilitator accuracy notes for tricky topics such as tokens, context windows and usage limits. Beginner test-run of every draft. Evidence base behind format choices: active learning (Freeman et al., 2014), spaced practice and self-testing (Dunlosky et al., 2013), learning by teaching (Fiorella and Mayer, 2013), student AI use survey (Digital Education Council, 2024); AI literacy competencies (Long and Magerko, 2020), productive failure (Kapur, 2016), the "jagged frontier" field experiment with consultants (Dell'Acqua and others) and India's data protection law with its 2025 Rules. Retention tracker. Open suggestion box.
Name a Radar Editor and two checkers.
First week of each month: publish the Radar.
One week and 24 hours before each session: run the vetting checklist and record the result in the session page.
Before any session that states facts about AI or law, a checker verifies sources and dates (including the data-protection dates in Session 14).
Record rejected tools and why.
Shared template, checklist form, access to tools' own documentation pages.
Research Desk (Radar Editor plus two checkers); Curation Lead.
Monthly Radar; per-session vetting; mid-year review.
Fewer broken sessions, accurate content, a visible research culture.
Radar published every month; zero sessions cancelled for tool failure; share of sessions with a completed vetting record; corrections issued per term.
Make projects non-scary: give every member a problem, a step-by-step ladder and a public stage.

fields.label: Why the club should do it

items.t: A problem card is carried through the year; a four-rung ladder structures the projects; projects must serve a business problem; and follow-up work is kept light.
All members; mixed-skill teams of three to five at the top rungs.

Problem Board where anyone posts a campus or community problem at any time (mess feedback, deadlines, placements, attendance, hostel, clubs, food waste, civic issues, local tourism information); Problem Cards from Session 10 and a Plan Card (who has the problem, what we will try, which tool, how we will know it worked). Project ladder: Rung 1 micro-project (30 minutes, in a session); Rung 2 mini-project (one to two weeks, solo or pair, no code: deadline tracker, mess-feedback summariser, club FAQ bot); Rung 3 team project (six to eight weeks, teams of three to five with mixed skills and a mentor: campus Q and A assistant, placement mock-interview bot, event auto-poster, syllabus-to-quiz generator, mess-feedback dashboard; output is a demo, a repository and a one-page write-up); Rung 4 Demo Day with judges. Real-person test (interview and feedback quote) at Rung 2 or 3. Squads self-formed by interest or by skill mix at a pitch night. Mentor per team and four-week milestone plans. Bug Bash where teams try to break each other's prototypes. Project portfolio page per project.
Open the board in Month 1.
Session 10: Annoyance Auction and Problem Cards.
Session 11: AI critic round and concept note v2.
Term 3: Rung 2 mini-projects (see V1-09 and V1-12 for support sessions).
Term 4: teams form (skill mix); mentors assigned; four-week milestone plans; fortnightly check-ins.
Session 23: Build Day. Session 24: Demo Day.
Shared board, Plan Card template, mentor list (seniors, alumni, faculty), starter kits (a template bot and an automation).
Projects Lead (owner); Mentors; Alumni Liaison (V2-06) for mentors; Faculty Advisor for approval of public demos.
Board always open; ladder runs Terms 2 to 4.
Most members or squads present a finished project with real-person feedback.
Problem Cards filed; real-person tests completed; projects shipped by Session 24; portfolio pages created.
Give management students competitive, case-style formats that test judgement, not just tool use.

fields.label: Why the club should do it

items.t: Case competitions and placements matter to a BMS cohort. Competitions are also the cheapest rehearsal for Neural Fest.
Teams of four or five, BMS and MBA mixed, first years with seniors.

Zero Rupee Consultant (Session 12): invented case, paper-only block, planted false claim, judge and returned scorecards. AI in the Real World case night (Session 10). Ad Auction (Session 21). AI on Trial courtroom (Session 16). Hallucination Face-off and Prompt Wars (Sessions 2 and 5). IPL prediction challenge: pairs write their own winner-picking rule in a spreadsheet using a public Kaggle dataset and climb an in-room leaderboard (optional bank session). Shark Tank with AI sharks (Session 11). Ridiculous Idea to Real Business (random problem, customer and constraint) with the E&I Cell as jury (bank). Startup pitch night. AI Capstone problem statements.
Write each case in plain English with every term footnoted; mark invented figures as invented.
No real campus vendor is analysed.
Brief judges in advance; publish the rubric; return scorecards.
Put a planted false claim in at least one case and run the reveal.
Provide a paper version if the network fails.
Case packs, rubric, judges (senior or faculty; industry guest by video), timer, hall.
Case Lead; judges recruited by Outreach (V2-04, V2-05); co-hosts from campus clubs (V2-07).
Sessions 10, 11, 12, 16, 21 in the core calendar; bank formats as extras.
Case-solving habits, judgement under time pressure, and public proof of skill.
Share of teams catching the planted claim; participants returning for a second competition; judge feedback scores.
Let everyone who joined at zero build something and show it to a room in a single day.

fields.label: Why the club should do it

items.t: The whole year builds towards it; teams get a three-hour build around the problem card; capstone problem statements are supplied; and a launch day gives a live link.
Up to about fifteen teams of three or four, mixing second years and juniors.

Tracks: study, campus life, business and operations, creative work, and data on a public dataset. Schedule: 10:00 check-in and rules (no-code or low-code, honest about limits); tool refresher and problem check with a mentor; build sprint 1 with mentors rotating every 20 minutes; lunch and a 60-second halfway show; build sprint 2 with submission at 16:00; three-minute demos with two for questions, scored on usefulness and clarity; judging while the audience votes; awards, group photo and a recap of the year. Each team names one way its tool could be misused before the awards. Starter kits for stalled teams. Optional launch lane for teams that want a live link: put the code in a repository and publish through a free host, supported by Maker Track coaches.
Four weeks out: confirm hall, power strips, backup hotspots, mentors, judges and prizes (with Outreach, V2-09).
Two weeks out: teams form from Problem Cards; scope to a one-day version.
On the day: follow the schedule; judging sheet rewards clarity and honesty about limits as much as polish.
Within five days: recap, thank-yous to mentors and sponsors, and a published list of projects.
Large hall with long tables, power strips, wifi plus hotspot backup, mentor list, submission form, judging sheet, prizes, starter kits.
Projects Lead (owner); Outreach Lead for judges, sponsors and prizes; mentors from seniors and alumni.
Once a year (Session 23).
Most teams submit a working demo; most members report building something for the first time.
Share of teams submitting a demo; share of members reporting a first build; judge scores; audience vote participation.

initiatives.title: Neural Fest: hackathon and Demo Day (Session 24)

items.t: Run one campus-wide event that the club could be judged by in three years: a one-day festival open to teams from outside, with a track for every kind of member.

fields.label: Why the club should do it

items.t: A hackathon with three tracks lets non-coders compete on level terms; a Demo Day is judged by industry; awards close the event; and peer clubs and platforms could co-host.
The whole institute and teams from other institutes (online for the pitch tracks).

Three tracks: Think It (best idea, pitched, nothing to build); Build It (best working thing, however it was made); Sell It (strongest business case behind someone else's build). Outside teams join Think It and Sell It online against the same rubric; Build It stays on campus. Industry judges and problem setters in year one, not banner sponsors. Awards by level, certificates and silly awards; peer vote and People's Choice; Demo Day with industry and faculty judges; Showcase booths with invited guests; handover of the Field Guide. Rehearsal: Session 12 opened to two outside teams online.
Treat as a proposal until the institute approves, a room and an exam-free date are fixed, and a term of smaller sessions is behind the club.
Four weeks of lead time: registration, team formation and two mentoring evenings inside normal slots.
Route every company approach through the Industrial Relations and Sponsorship Committee first (V2-07).
Use a platform listing (V2-09) for registration if offered.
Do not describe the festival as booked until it is.
Hall, judges, rubric, registration form or platform listing, prizes, certificates, volunteers, media coverage.
Projects Lead and Outreach Lead jointly; Faculty Advisor; E&I Cell mentors and judges; Media Cell.
Once, in Month 12; rehearsal at Session 12.
A signature event, outside participation, partner visibility and a portfolio of demos.
Registrations (campus and outside); judges and problem statements secured; entries per track; participant feedback; media pieces published.
Offer a deeper route for members who want technical depth, without making the core programme intimidating.

fields.label: Why the club should do it

items.t: The core deliberately has no coding track, to keep BMS students in the room, yet there is strong advanced material (terminals, APIs, local models, RAG, deployment). The solution is a separate optional track.
Members who have completed Terms 1 and 2 and want to go further; small cohort of about 10 to 20 (assumed, [Added in synthesis]).

Electives: Terminal in 15 minutes and local models (pwd, ls, cd, mkdir, cat; a small model running offline; privacy and cost reasons); What is an API? (restaurant analogy, calling public APIs without code) and Your first AI API call (an API key and a ready-made notebook that turns twenty product reviews into a sentiment table); RAG explained through own documents (embeddings, vector databases, retrieval) and customising AI (custom GPTs, knowledge bases, what fine-tuning is and when it helps); LLMs inside: tokens, context windows, training, inference, hallucinations; Launch Day: put the project in a repository over a secure key and publish it with a free host to get a live link, with the vocabulary card (repository, commit, push, key pair, deploy); Agents with supervision; Build-a-Bot Battle; Python without learning Python.
Run as optional evening labs after Term 2, not in the core calendar.
Provide a fallback lane for every environment-dependent step (the Launch Day plan's own success check expects about 70% to complete the secure-key step and the rest to use a fallback).
Pre-work is stated up front (accounts, installed tools).
Mentors are Maker-level seniors and alumni.
Laptops, accounts for a repository host and a deployment host, a local-model app, notebooks, mentors.
Maker Track Lead; Mentors; Curation Lead.
Four to six optional labs between Months 6 and 11.
A group of members able to build and deploy, and mentor others.
Live links published; labs completed; mentors produced; self-rated confidence before and after.
Convert learning into employability: sharper CVs, practice interviews and visible project portfolios.

fields.label: Why the club should do it

items.t: The Career Lab ends the plan with Build and Get Hired; a CV session is included; and AI is tied to management careers.
Members preparing for internships and placements, especially second-year students.

Six Seconds on Your CV: a sharper CV, a LinkedIn headline and a practice interview, with a Training and Development Cell volunteer vetting against the checklist used on campus. Careers panel with alumni and industry on roles, skills and portfolios. Internship and careers info session with partner companies. Project portfolio pages and GitHub or demo links from V1-08. Placement mock-interview bot and Using AI without getting caught (integrity, privacy, bias, over-reliance as a campus-scenario debate) as bank topics.
Agree a slot with the Training and Development Cell; ask for a volunteer and their checklist.
Source panellists via V2-06 and V2-04.
Run the CV session in Term 4 as an extra, not one of the 24.
Record outcomes (interviews or internships reported).
CV templates, practice-interview prompts, T and D Cell volunteers, panel hall.
Careers Lead; Alumni Liaison; T and D Cell.
One CV session, one panel and one info session in Terms 3 and 4.
Better CVs, portfolio links and internship leads.
CVs reviewed; interviews or internships reported; panel attendance.

initiatives.title: Feedback, Evaluation and Continuous Improvement Loop

items.t: Check that the programme works at three levels (per session, mid-year, end of year) and change it when it does not.

fields.label: Why the club should do it

items.t: A plan with no way of being wrong is only a wish, so specific measures are set; evaluation stays light so a fun session is not turned into administration.
Curation Lead and Core team; members as respondents.

Every session: a one-line slip ("the one thing from tonight you will use this week") plus three counts on the back of the attendance sheet (how many came, how many were new, how many were also there last time); a three-question poll (understood? enjoyed? what next?) via QR code; next-morning one-page record with numbers, what broke, what to change and the best slip. Mid-year review after Session 12: the first twelve go side by side; a session stays if most of its room could do the thing at the end, otherwise it is rebuilt. Retention tracker by person and session type. End of year: the twenty-four pages and the slips become one handover. Measures: Session 12 attendance at least 70% of Session 1; exit-poll agreement targets of 80% and 90% for "I learned a use I didn't know"; confidence before and after; share who spoke at least once and how many moved per debate statement; content reach.
Print the slip and counts template before Session 1.
Collect slips at the door; read them before planning the next session.
File the session record by 10:00 the next day.
Hold the mid-year review within two weeks of Session 12 and publish its decisions to the club.
Use feedback to improve sessions, never to rank members.
Slip template, poll form, shared folder.
Quality Lead (owner); Curation Lead; all hosts.
Per session; mid-year; annual.
Evidence-based changes; early warning on drift; a handover that starts from what happened.
Share of sessions with a filed record; response rates; number of changes made after the review.
Protect members, partners and the club through a short, enforced code of practice.

fields.label: Why the club should do it

items.t: Nearly every plan needs a safeguard line. Writing them once avoids contradictory rules and protects the club's reputation, which Outreach depends on.
Hosts, members, guests and partners.

Rules: no personal data, passwords, marks, bank details or confidential college information in public tools; nobody is featured, imitated or cloned by AI without agreeing, and humour stays kind; no voice cloning, no editing real photos of others without permission, existing songs only as inspiration; no real person's photograph, voice or name in generated texts; detectors are never used to accuse a classmate; disclose AI-assisted work and follow the college's academic-integrity policy; public documents only in finance sessions and no investment, tax or loan advice; free tools only and each tool's age requirements respected; recordings and posts only with consent and with demo accounts and fictional examples where possible; sessions state "what we will not do" out loud.
Adopt the code at the first committee meeting; faculty advisor signs off.
Read the rules aloud at the start of each session.
Give hosts a one-page "if it goes wrong" card.
Report incidents to the Quality Lead within 24 hours.
One-page code, consent form template, incident log.
Quality Lead (owner); Faculty Advisor; all hosts.
Adopted once; reviewed at the mid-year review.
A safe, trusted environment and no preventable incidents.
Incidents logged; consent forms on file for all public content; code read aloud at 100% of sessions.
Make the programme survive exams, low turnout, tool failure and a change of committee.

fields.label: Why the club should do it

items.t: Contingencies are set out with care; risk tables and an exam rule are included. Documenting them up front prevents quiet erosion in February.
Committee; incoming team.

Contingency table (Part 4, Section 4.8): twelve people instead of eighty (table mode, three-team quiz, two-team case); network down (paper versions; model file pre-loaded on a pen drive); nobody has a laptop (teams of three or four around one machine, or a lab for the seven keyboard sessions); tools change (backup tool and screenshots per station). Calendar rule for exams. 12-session fallback. Risks and tweaks table, including mid-year drift, toxic leaderboard, same voices, tools, fizzling projects, odd numbers and privacy. Handover pack: 24 session pages, slips, Field Guide v2.0, partner ledger and outreach pack, a list of what worked and what did not.
Approve the fallback list at the first committee meeting.
Review conditions monthly: turnout, calendar, tool health.
Trigger the fallback by the stated rule and tell the club why.
Prepare the handover pack from Month 10.
Shared folder, pen drive, backup hotspots.
Programme Coordinator; Quality Lead; Curation Lead.
Monthly condition check; handover in Month 12.
No silent shrinkage; smooth transition between cohorts.
Fallback decisions made on stated rules; handover pack complete before the final session.
